Speech by First Secretary of State Louise Haigh at the Confederation of British Industry Annual Conference 2026

Thank you to Rain and to the CBI for inviting me to speak with you today.

I was incredibly proud to have the voice of British business join us in Brussels on Friday.

And grateful for the full-throated backing you gave the Prime Minister and the ambitious deal he agreed with the EU…

As the deal you have championed for many years was agreed.

A deal that will bring down the cost of business, help with the cost of food, reduce needless red tape, and reduce friction with our nearest and largest trading partner.

When Andy Burnham became Prime Minister…

It was obvious that the Made in Europe policy posed serious risks to the UK’s critical industries including automotive and steel…

Both fundamental to this government’s

Everyone told us that getting Made in Europe on the agenda at this summit would be impossible. But thanks to the Prime Minister’s ambition and courage in taking this debate on, we have a far better deal for Britain

I think it is important to note both the psychological as well as the economic impact that Friday’s deal will have on business both in Britain and Europe…

And I join Rain in her encouragement to remove our gloom tinted glasses and be more ambitious for Britain.

I recognise that, for many of you…

Business leaders, employers, investors…

Opening the CBI Annual Conference with a keynote speech on public control may feel somewhat counterintuitive

But I’m going to ask you to suspend that scepticism To park any preconceptions you have.

Because at the heart of the argument I hope to make today…

Is a belief that genuine and enduring collaboration between public and private sectors is the only way to rewire our economy…

To drive good growth in every postcode…

And to deliver the meaningful change our country is crying out for.

But I will start by saying something about where we find ourselves today.

Because the UK economy has performed far better than many had predicted…

Growth of 0.7% between July and September. When conflict in the Middle East has pushed up costs around the world.

As the Chancellor said, Britain is showing standout resilience.

More than 34 and a half million people are in work. And unemployment is lower than a year ago.

That resilience didn’t come from nowhere.

It’s the grit, tenacity and adaptability of the private sector.

Workers and managers, entrepreneurs and investors. All striving. Many of you in this room.

A pandemic. An energy shock. War in Europe. And now conflict in the Middle East.

But resilience is not the same as success.

And we cannot accept muddling along any more. If we ever thought otherwise, we must now be in no doubt.

Let alone the prosperity we want for our children and grandchildren.

Of fracturing trading relationships…

Of a ferocious race for technology…

We must compete harder than ever for our place in the world.

And there is real cause for optimism.

Britain is a nation of innovators.

We have produced around 200 ‘unicorn’ companies. Behind only the US and China.

Last year, we attracted more technology investment than any other country in Europe.

Our universities are among the best in the world. One of our great exports.

Our culture is enjoyed in every corner of the globe. Most countries look at those strengths with envy. They were built over decades, if not centuries.

Our frontier isn’t the problem.

The cost of energy. The cost of housing. The cost of getting to work.

How concentrated power and decision-making are. And yet how weak, how slow, and even obstructive our institutions and Westminster politics can be. So much grit in the wheels.

Every day you spend filling in new forms to export, waiting for a planning consent or a grid connection, is a

day your capital sits idle and you are not bringing in revenue.

But if we get the basics right…

We have all the ingredients of a confident, competitive and modern economy.

The Prime Minister’s diagnosis of what holds us back is clear.

With too many places stripped of the power to back their own strengths.

Second, essential services were privatised. Monopolies either left unchallenged…

Or systems split apart, creating complexity. And third, accountability outsourced.

To unelected regulators and arm’s-length bodies.

So politicians could point somewhere else when things went wrong.

And the public could never quite see who was in charge.

Now, I know the word “privatisation” can start an argument.

This is not about whether markets work. They do. Where there is genuine competition, as in telecoms, markets have given consumers choice, and kept prices low while delivering infrastructure.

The social license to operate must be won every day, by building trust and having the best value product or service.

Where competition exists, it should be left to thrive.

Supported by our strong, independent Competition and Markets Authority.

But when it comes to essential services, we have spent four decades trying and failing to recreate market conditions when consumers have no alternative. Public control is about getting the right outcomes. It is not ideological. Ownership is not a requirement. We took the railway back into public ownership because it was not working for passengers or the taxpayer… But we want Great British Railways to be challenged by Open Access operators

In Greater Manchester’s Bee Network, routes are set by the elected Mayor to benefit the community The services are still run by private operators. Delivering the homes we need depends on a buoyant developer sector

Looking at water and energy, we must accept that… The status quo is not the neutral, pragmatic centre ground.

It’s the outlier. An exception that no other nation is trying to emulate.

Around the world, the core infrastructure of water overwhelmingly stays in public hands.

England is almost unique in handing the entire system to private owners.

The only other country in that corner with us is Chile. There was something of a meeting of minds between those two governments in the 1980s.

We are also one of the few countries in Europe whose electricity and gas transmission networks are entirely privately owned.

Foreign governments now own a bigger share of our utilities than the British government does.

Significant stakes in our water, electricity and gas networks.

Returns paid to their taxpayers.

I welcome that investment. Let me be clear about that. But it raises a question.

Why do other governments see the strategic and commercial value in holding Britain’s essential assets… When for forty years, the British government couldn’t? And it isn’t just Europe.

Look at the United States of America. Hardly a hotbed of state socialism.

Most Americans get their water from a public utility. Fewer than one in ten get it from a private one.

Community-owned power companies serve one in seven American electricity customers.

In Los Angeles. In Seattle. In Nashville. In Austin. And the federal government still owns the Tennessee Valley Authority, one of the biggest power companies in the country.

Nobody thinks America is anti-business.

So, let’s be honest with ourselves.

The status quo is the ideological position.

And saying so should not be taboo.

To make the experiment work, successive governments leant on regulation.

First, to try to recreate competition for monopolies through a spreadsheet.

Then to manage what private markets would never price in on their own. Like the spare capacity that keeps the lights on.

Then to deliver social policy. Treated as a free good, because it went on the bill, not the budget.

Ofgem now has six times the staff it had in the early 2000s.

Almost three times the administrative budget in real terms.

And a rulebook more than six times longer. We’ve built a hulking, complex behemoth of a regulatory state.

It satisfies no one. Not consumers. Not investors. When you prioritise everything, you prioritise nothing. In the fog of complexity, bad actors can thrive…

While the rest of us can’t move with the clarity and pace this moment demands.

That is why public control should not alarm anyone in this room.

It’s not ideological. It’s pragmatic and it’s essential. For people. For places. And for business.

We will measure our progress against three tests. Affordability. Investability. Accountability.

Essential services, more accessible and affordable for businesses and households.

A new partnership with private capital. Clear rules. Clear expectations. A fair return. Good actors backed to succeed.

Legitimacy restored, with faster decisions, made closer to the people and businesses they affect and politicians accountable for trade-offs.

When it comes to energy, British business is competing on an uneven playing field.

We have the highest industrial energy prices among advanced economies.

That is not the kind of exceptionalism we’re aiming for. In 2008, UK industrial electricity prices were around 23% above the median for the EU14 and the UK. By 2025, they were more than double.

You know what that means better than I do. One in four British manufacturers say they’ve moved production abroad, or are seriously considering it, because of energy prices.

Every time fossil fuel prices spike, we get poorer. Output from our energy-intensive industries fell by around a third between 2021 and 2024.

And the prize for fixing it is enormous.

CBI research found that a reducing industrial energy costs by 20% would unlock £130 billion of economic output

We cannot reindustrialise this country without tackling the cost of energy.

We expanded the supercharger scheme for heavy industry.

Through the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme, 10,000 manufacturers can take up to £40 per megawatt hour off their bills from April.

Applications close in one week. If you’re eligible and you haven’t applied, please do.

But subsidising prices for one part of industry is no substitute for fixing the system.

So our approach rests on three big shifts.

First, taking costs off of the bill.

Rachel Reeves already took £150 of costs off bills by slashing the Renewable Obligation

At the Budget, the Chancellor scrapped plans for a new levy on gas bills – the Gas Shipper Obligation Both funded instead by the Exchequer

And we have committed to implement a new Cost Control Framework

Second, building an energy system for the benefit of its users, not producers.

That means prioritising cheap, clean power. Stimulating demand. Accelerating electrification.

Because the surest route to net zero is electricity people can afford to use.

It means accelerating and prioritising grid connections for factories, hospitals, homes and, yes, data centres. Spreading out the cost of the network.

And it means building the right things, in the right places. Last year, bill payers spent £2 billion switching off wind farms…

While paying to switch on gas plants somewhere else. So we’ll get smarter about when and where new generation is deployed, and build-out the network in line with demand.

No more paying for power we can’t use.

Third, breaking the link between the price of electricity and the price of gas.

Clean power producers should not earn windfall returns simply because gas is expensive.

And gas plants should not be able to exploit the nation’s moments of need for excess profit.

That is our plan for the decade. To bring energy bills in line with our European counterparts by the middle of the next decade.

Britain tops another OECD table.

We spend 1.4% of our GDP on housing allowances. The highest of any OECD country.

Councils’ net spending on temporary accommodation has risen ten-fold in 15 years, to £1.5 billion. That is a transfer from taxpayers, including the businesses in this room, to the private rented sector.

Meanwhile central government sits on millions of acres of land

Enough to build hundreds of thousands of homes An asset for the public sector and foundation for families Building homes we need is not something the state can do by itself

And a strong private market means more social rent homes, and a weaker one means fewer

So when conditions become as difficult as they are now, that’s a shared problem, and we’ve heard the call to act There’s no silver bullet, but over the coming weeks we will set out steps to make the system faster, reduce uncertainty and tackle costs.

Which brings me to investability.

One of the most important ways to keep housing and infrastructure affordable is to pay the lowest possible cost of capital.

Whether it is public money or private money Every extra point on the cost of capital for a grid upgrade, a reservoir, or a new wind farm ends up on somebody’s bill.

That is why this government is so resolute in our commitment to reducing the UK budget deficit and stabilising debt, consistent with our fiscal rules. And why we must insulate ourselves from imported inflation and bear down on the cost of business by focusing on cheap domestic energy

Government, and politics, also has a responsibility for reinforcing public interest.

Because when a sector loses public trust, political risk goes up.

And so does the cost of capital. For everyone. Prices feed back into public dissatisfaction. It becomes a vicious cycle to break out of.

When it comes to the water sector as a whole, the public are furious.

Sewage in rivers, lakes and beaches. Clean water is wasted to leaks. New homes blocked by a lack of supply.

We were told that privatisation would unlock necessary investment, because it would no longer be competing with schools and hospitals for taxpayer money. £55 billion taken in dividends.

Gearing shot up from 4% to 66% today.

It will be a long-term project to right the wrong turn… To make water boring again.

We will partner with those in the sector who are committed to see it through

Clarity. Certainty. Consistency. A fair deal.

And I want to say clearly, on the record: we are committed to ensuring the whole of the water industry works in the public interest.

The Cunliffe recommendations which strengthen the parts of the sector that work well will be the starting point for our Water Bill

Including streamlined planning, a supervisory model of regulation, and a single independent regulator with a clear focus.

Re-legitimising the water industry. For good. That’s our aim.

To everyone who shares it, we will back you to succeed. To deliver the much needed investment after years of neglect

And reform how we deliver outcomes and value for consumers

Bills are set to rise by 36% between 2025 and 2030. Without intervention, we risk even larger rises at the next price review.

Where nature-based solutions can meet or beat planned environmental improvements, we will use them. Restoring wetlands. Managing whole catchments. Working with the land, not against it.

At a fraction of the cost of concrete.

With real benefits for carbon and for biodiversity. …

We’ve taken the same approach to data centres. Clear rules and expectations.

Pay your fair share of energy costs. Invest in the community. Create good jobs and apprenticeships. Strengthen our security. Meet environmental standards. If you meet our public interest tests, we will back you. …

The government should also take stakes where it serves a purpose

Sizewell C, once operational, will generate enough electricity to power 6 million homes

It is too big and risky for the private sector to finance alone.

Partnership brought private capital but also delivery expertise to help make the project a success I have heard first hand from our partners La Caisse how much they value having one government alongside them at every stage of the project

And, with skin in the game, government has been more motivated to reform the needless regulation faced by the nuclear industry

We will deliver the Fingleton reforms as committed to. In full.

To deliver the new nuclear fleet for our energy security To renew the nuclear deterrent which keeps us safe And to win the high value manufacturing jobs from commercialising SMRs

The Nuclear Regulation Bill we bring forward in the new year will also include reforms to judicial review… Because the risk of legal challenge is a chill factor, that motivates ever more complex consultation and leaves essential projects in limbo.

And we will empower Parliament to designate and authorise the country’s most critical infrastructure projects.

When challenge is unavoidable, for the most critical projects, we will offer indemnities so that developers do not down tools

That’s what public control offers…

An opportunity for stability and certainty… For national renewal through public and private investment

Clarity in place of churn. A fair return in place of a free for-all.

And a government that wants you to succeed. Giving business the confidence to invest here, and create good jobs in our industrial heartlands. Creating good quality jobs in all parts of the country. The role of the private sector is essential to fulfilling that. That is why I am delighted to announce today a new Northern Economy and Reindustrialisation Commissioner.

With an impeccable industrial career we can learn much from.

Juergen will be based in No 10 North.

He will report to the Business Secretary and I, implementing our reindustrialisation agenda… And crucially on linking with business and leveraging private capital.

I am delighted he has taken on this crucial role.

Our expectation, in return, is accountability. All of those here who operate in genuine competitive markets

You are accountable every single day. There is no ducking it.

Product quality, customer service, supply chains, operational efficiency

Finely balanced judgements between risk and opportunity cost. Growth and consolidation. Any slip up could cost your employees their jobs and your investors’ money.

Now consider our monopoly operators.

In 2023, the average wait for a grid connection was five years.

What’s worse is just 14 percent of projects got the connection date they asked for

Imagine telling your customers that was what you were offering. You would expect to lose them.

But if you need electricity, you have nowhere else to go.

You just have to sit and wait it out.

The grid has every incentive to build out the connections - they get a guaranteed return on what they invest But then again, they get paid either way, so why take any risk of buying kit ahead of time

So we will change the incentives

By introducing competition into the build out of our network, including through Great British Grid, and allowing developers to build their own connections.

And by imposing tougher penalties on network companies that fail to deliver a grid slot on time. If you promise a connection, you deliver the connection. Between November 2024 and June 2025, the demand waiting to connect tripled, to 125 gigawatts Much of that is speculative bids by land promoters

So we will cut the chancers and prioritise the connections we really need.

But accountability is a two-way street

The Prime Minister is clear eyed about the limitations of centralised government, and the failings of politics. That is why we are rewiring the state.

Over decades, politicians were content to duck accountability by giving responsibility away from ministers to a sprawling web of regulators and arm’s length bodies.

More than twenty statutory consultees, all with veto power…

Notionally bound by statutory deadlines, but obfuscation has become habitual.

Decisions that affect your business, taken by bodies you can’t hold to account.

And I am not blaming the officials in these organisations. Risk aversion is a learned behaviour

Better to not let something happen than risk it going wrong

But the missed opportunities are a cost to society and they all add up

So I am sending a clear message to our public servants We accept a higher level of risk and the buck stops with us.

Be bold, be fast and make things happen.

We’ve already upped our tolerance for legal risk and reduced the amount of consultations

In procurement, social value had become a coat hook for every government issue to the point of being meaningless

So we stripped it right back, so our priorities are clear for you to meet

Good jobs and skills training for workers here in Britain. That’s it.

And as part of rewiring the state we will reform arm’s length bodies to increase public control

We will take a look at each of their functions and pose the challenge: what should be devolved, what can be dissolved and what could be delivered departments We’ve already begun that process with the Environment Agency, Natural England, Ofwat and the Drinking Water Inspectorate

Where decisions are intrinsic to the fabric of a place, those powers and responsibilities must be made in that place, not in Whitehall

Because if a decision can be taken closer to the people it affects, that is where we want it taken.

We are building real capability in our strategic authorities.

With the powers and funding to join up transport, housing, skills and planning in their places. And the CBI’s new secondment scheme will have real impact.

It is so vital that we have the help of experienced business professionals as we rewire the state for good. To anyone here that wants to make a difference to where you live, or where you grew up, now is the time.

And for a business wanting to expand, we want you to have one door to knock on.

And local leaders who can say yes, and make it happen.

So let me return to where I started.

Adam Smith knew that a monopoly is not a market. For forty years, we pretended otherwise in the things that matter most.

And British business has paid the price.

In the highest industrial electricity prices among advanced economies.

In five-year waits for the grid.

In homes and labs that couldn’t be built for want of water.

In workers priced out of the places where the jobs are. Time is a tax, paid by British businesses for too long. This government will change course.

Put pragmatism and public interest ahead of failed political ideology.

Public control is not anti-business.

It’s about getting the foundations right, so private enterprise can do what it does best.

It doesn’t take Britain somewhere radical.

It moves us towards the mainstream.

Affordable. Investable. Accountable.

These are the tests we have set ourselves. And we want to achieve them by working with you.

Not as critics on the sidelines. But in collaboration, as partners, building it together.

Because when Britain’s foundations are strong, British business is unstoppable.

Do not include personal or financial information like your National Insurance number or credit card details.
